title: Donald Trump’s Tariff Re-Do in Southeast Asia
gist: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down in February the sweeping tariffs of up to 49 percent that Washington imposed on trade partners based on bilateral surplus size, leaving Indonesia and Malaysia holding hastily signed reciprocal trade deals full of provisions the author judges unenforceable.

insights.claim: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down the sweeping tariffs in February, invalidating the trade regime the U.S. had imposed on partners worldwide the prior year.
insights.speaker: James Guild
insights.so_what: Legal invalidation is the key regime break — any tariff re-imposition must run through a different statutory route, creating a window of policy uncertainty for Asian exporters.
insights.quote: In any case, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the tariffs in February.
insights.locator: In any case, the U.S. Supreme Court

insights.claim: The struck-down U.S. tariffs went as high as 49 percent and were calibrated largely to the size of each country's bilateral trade surplus with the United States rather than to any sectoral or security logic.
insights.speaker: James Guild
insights.so_what: A bilateral-surplus formula means exposure is mechanically predictable from trade balance data — screen surplus-heavy exporters first for any revived tariff scheme.
insights.quote: The tariffs, which went as high as 49 percent, were based largely on the size of each country’s bilateral trade surplus with the United States.
insights.locator: Last year, the United States imposed sweeping tariffs

insights.claim: Thailand and Vietnam, as very large exporters to the U.S., faced the stiffest tariff rates under the surplus-based formula.
insights.speaker: James Guild
insights.so_what: Thai and Vietnamese export names carry the highest beta to any reinstatement of U.S. surplus-linked tariffs.
insights.locator: Really big exporters, like Thailand and Vietnam

insights.claim: Indonesia and Malaysia moved quickly to sign lopsided reciprocal trade agreements with the U.S. to cut their tariffs below 20 percent, a concession that looks premature now that the underlying tariffs have been voided.
insights.speaker: James Guild
insights.so_what: First movers in trade negotiations paid real concessions for relief that litigation delivered for free — a cautionary template for the next tariff round.
insights.quote: Indonesia and Malaysia quickly agreed to lopsided reciprocal trade agreements with the U.S. to get the tariffs lowered to under 20 percent. That may have been hasty

insights.claim: The Indonesian and Malaysian deals contain numerous provisions that are seemingly impossible to enforce, implying the agreements may prove hollow in practice even if they remain formally in force.
insights.speaker: James Guild
insights.so_what: Discount headline commitments in these bilateral deals when modeling Indonesian and Malaysian trade flows; enforcement gaps mean limited real-economy effect.
